BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r1.claim: The interrogative hamza denies that anyone should wish this, unlike a question denying an act already occurring; he illustrates the difference with two Arabic examples.

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r2.claim: A garden can mean its dense trees; if it means the land containing them, trees must be supplied for rivers to flow beneath them.

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r3.claim: The syntax of ‘all fruits’ makes it a description of provision, as in the phrase ‘each of us has an assigned station.’

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r4.claim: ‘All fruits’ means a great variety, not literally every fruit, as in the promise of every kind of fruit in Paradise.

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r5.claim: Palms and grapes are singled out as the noblest and most useful trees; other trees are included by giving these prominence.

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r6.claim: Old age intensifies need for the garden's benefits while making it harder to earn a living; weak young dependents cannot work or support the owner.

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r7.claim: The whirlwind is a violent revolving wind rising from the ground toward the sky like a column, carrying fire that ruins the garden.

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r8.claim: The parable depicts Judgment Day grief when good deeds are cancelled by ostentation or injury just when their doer needs them.

BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p348#2/r9.claim: Its spiritual parallel is the seeker who reaches the unseen realm, then turns back to illusion and makes his effort vain.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p349/r1.claim: ‘Thus’ points back to clear explanations of striving and spending for God and the stories of Abraham and Ezra; the signs establish monotheism and the truth of religion.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p349/r2.claim: The signs call readers to reflect, learn from their lessons, and act accordingly.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r3.speaker: القشيري
BURSEVI:v1p349/r3.claim: Qushayrī contrasts sincere and hypocritical spending: some receive replacement and honor, while others waste, lose their wealth, and have their deeds nullified.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r4.speaker: القشيري
BURSEVI:v1p349/r4.claim: Qushayrī likens faithful deeds to a flourishing crop and failed deeds to a ruined bargain that leaves an old person without income.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p349/r5.claim: Works need sincerity because their fruits depend on their root.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r6.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
BURSEVI:v1p349/r6.claim: Muʿādh reports that, when he was sent to Yemen, the Prophet advised him to make his religion sincere, making a little work sufficient.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p349/r7.claim: Treat ostentation by removing its roots and establishing its opposite; its main causes are love of this world and preferring immediate pleasure to the afterlife.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p349/r8.claim: Before each worship act, inspect the heart, remove thoughts of ostentation, resolve on sincerity, and keep resisting them.

BURSEVI:v1p349/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p349/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p349/r9.claim: Ostentation enters in three stages: expecting people to notice, wanting their praise and status, then accepting and settling on that desire; reject each.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:266-267/r1.claim: The garden depicts any good deed, including charity, done for God's pleasure when the ego later emerges; conflicting ego motions become a whirlwind seized by Satan for whispering.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:266-267/r2.claim: Self-regard or ostentation is like fire that consumes the deed precisely when it is most needed.

QASHANI:2:266-267/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:266-267/r3.speaker: أمير المؤمنين علي عليه السلام
QASHANI:2:266-267/r3.claim: ʿAlī asks God to forgive acts of devotion whose intentions his heart later contradicted.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108/r1.claim: Qatada's parable depicts an elderly owner, too weak to earn and supporting weak dependents, losing his fruitful garden just when he most needs it; a scorching wind burns it.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108/r2.speaker: الحسن
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p108/r2.claim: Hasan says the destructive whirlwind was bitter cold, which burned and ruined the garden when its owner needed it most, like lost good deeds.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p109/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p109/r1.speaker: مجاهد
ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p109/r1.claim: Mujahid explains the call to reflect as a call to obey.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r3.claim: نخيل is a collective or broken plural like نخل; al-Rāghib derives it from the trees’ selection and notes the date palm’s distinctive pollination and growth.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r4.claim: عنب is a collective name for grapes, with عنبة as its singular; أعناب is its plural and عنباء is another extended form.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r5.speaker: الزجاج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r5.claim: Al-Zajjāj describes إعصار as a powerful whirlwind that raises dust toward the sky; another view identifies it as a deadly hot wind that compresses clouds.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p651/r6.claim: احتراق is intransitive, while أحرقت is transitive; حرق ناب can describe a man’s tooth grinding in anger, with a cited line read using either nominative or accusative ناب.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r1.speaker: السدي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r1.claim: He takes the final garden parable as another image of the show-off.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r2.claim: He reads it as a parable for someone who reminds a recipient of charity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r3.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والربيع وغيرهم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r3.claim: They apply the parable to someone who falls short in obedience.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r4.speaker: ابن جريج
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r4.claim: He applies it to a person given youth and wealth who fails to act until both are taken away.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r5.claim: He compares many acts of obedience ending in a final sin to a garden ruined just when its elderly owner most needs it; a similar report is related from Umar.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r6.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r6.claim: Hasan says few understand this image: an old, weakened person with many children loses his garden when most dependent on it, just as people most need their deeds after worldly life ends.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r7.claim: The interrogative hamza conveys denial and improbability; أحد means any one of you distributively, not an item restricted by a negative construction.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r8.speaker: الحسن
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r8.claim: He reads جنات in the plural.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p671/r9.claim: Dates and grapes are singled out as the most honored and useful trees; the Qur'an names date palms while naming grapes by their fruit because every part of the palm is useful.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r1.claim: He analyzes the clause as a subject and predicate, then discusses competing parses for min.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r2.speaker: الأخفش
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r2.claim: He treats min in من كل الثمرات as extra, yielding له فيها كل الثمرات, with a generalizing expression rather than literal totality.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r3.claim: The author rejects extra min under Kufan and standard Basran conditions, and instead allows an omitted noun such as رزق or ثمرات before من كل الثمرات.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r4.claim: The apparent waw in وأصابه الكبر is circumstantial with an implied qad; alternative analyses take it as present meaning or as coordinated by sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r5.speaker: الفراء
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r5.claim: He allows the past clause because يود can take either أن or لو, letting one construction stand in place of the other.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r6.claim: He explains the coordination by the sense of wishing: would anyone wish to have a garden and be struck by old age?

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r7.claim: He rejects treating old age itself as something desired; the denial concerns the combination of owning a garden and being struck by old age.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p672/r8.claim: The word أصابه carries a stronger sense of impact than simply saying he grew old, as elsewhere in the garden and stone images.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r1.claim: Al-kibar means old age; ضعفاء and ضِعاف are plural forms of ضعيف, referring either to small children or needy dependents.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r2.claim: The masculine pronoun in فيه agrees with the masculine noun إعصار; نار is the subject of a preceding prepositional phrase or an omitted predicate.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r3.claim: The successive فاء suggests the whirlwind strikes after the garden has ripened and become useful; احترقت is the passive-effect counterpart to burning it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r4.claim: The fire in the whirlwind is the scorching wind; Ibn Masud reports that the jinn-creating samum is one seventieth of the Fire, while another explanation is lightning.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r5.speaker: الحسن والضحاك
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r5.claim: They understand a whirlwind containing fire as a wind containing cold, biting wind.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r6.claim: The parables are explanatory illustrations that make signs leading to truth understandable.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r7.claim: Reflection should turn people from transient worldly things toward what remains in the afterlife.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p673/r8.claim: The passage uses transitions from particular to general, allusion, simile, ellipsis, specification, parable, and metaphor.

AKHFASH:v1p200/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p200/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p200/r1.claim: ذرية ضعفاء and the other form ذرية ضعافا are equivalent plural forms; فعيل can take plurals like ظراف and ظرفاء.

FARRA:v1p175/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p175/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p175/r1.claim: After وددت, both أن and لو can introduce a future wish; this licenses a past-form verb such as فأصابها with future meaning under the implied لو.

FARRA:v1p175/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p175/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p175/r2.claim: Because إن and لو can both describe future conditions, Arabic sometimes answers one with the construction normally associated with the other.

FARRA:v1p175/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p175/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p175/r3.claim: Abu's reading of ود الذين كفروا has لو تغفلوا ... فيميلوا, matching the interpretation ودوا أن تفعلوا; raising فيميلون instead follows لو.

FARRA:v1p175/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p175/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p175/r4.claim: Arabic may combine different forms with overlapping meanings, such as ما with إن or اللاء with الذين; identical repeated forms are not licensed the same way.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r1.claim: The opening asks whether anyone would love this outcome; the hamza is reproachful, and a report says ʿUmar read yuḥibbu, ‘would love.’

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r2.claim: The garden is centered on palms and grapes, the most valuable core species, without excluding others; the Qur’an names the palm tree itself but grape fruit, perhaps because the palm is wholly useful.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r3.claim: Palm trees are analyzed either as a collective plural or a collective noun; grapes is the plural of ʿinaba, while ʿinbāʾ is a feminine-marked form that does not decline.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r4.claim: The expression janna may mean the dense trees themselves or land containing them; the first is more fitting because rivers run beneath it without supplying an omitted ‘trees.’

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r5.claim: In ‘he has therein of every fruit,’ the prepositional phrase can be a fronted predicate, while ‘of every fruit’ describes an omitted provision or fruit; min may be extra under al-Akhfash.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r6.claim: ‘Every fruit’ means many kinds rather than literally all; reading fruit as benefits or as general after the two named kinds is also discussed, with the latter rejected.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r7.claim: The garden owner is struck by old age, a more forceful expression than simply being old; the circumstantial clause highlights his urgent need and inability to restore his livelihood.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r8.speaker: الفراء، أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r8.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows the coordinated past tense to represent a future result; Abū Ḥayyān objects that this makes the old age part of the wish, which the author finds unconvincing to dismiss.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r9.claim: The weak offspring are dependents unable to earn a living; ḍuʿafāʾ is a plural of ḍaʿīf, and a variant reads ḍiʿāf.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p37/r10.claim: An iʿṣār is a rotating whirlwind, descending or rising, generated when competing air currents collide; it can grow strong enough to uproot trees or snatch boats.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r1.claim: The fire-bearing whirlwind is named and described for its rhetorical force; it may wrap like a twisted cloth or squeeze clouds and passing bodies, and tanwīn magnifies the fire.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets iʿṣār as any violent wind and its fire as the scorching samūm.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r3.claim: This image portrays the grief of a donor whose good deeds are nullified just when old and needy on Judgment Day, like an elderly parent losing the family’s garden.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r4.speaker: عطاء
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r4.claim: ʿAṭāʾ reports that ʿUmar asked about the parable; Ibn ʿAbbās explained a formerly righteous person who, near death and most in need of a good ending, commits sins and burns his deeds, impressing ʿUmar.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r5.claim: A version transmitted by al-Bukhārī, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Jarīr, and others has ʿUmar ask the Companions about the verse and Ibn ʿAbbās describe a rich obedient person corrupted by Satan until his deeds burn.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38/r6.claim: The Ibn ʿAbbās interpretation is stronger than limiting the parable to charity invalidated by reproach or ostentation, since he is the Qur’an’s interpreter and ʿUmar accepted it.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#2/r1.claim: The signs are explained clearly so people may reflect on their lessons, take heed, and act accordingly.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p38#2/r2.claim: Alternatively, people should direct thought to what perishes in this world and what endures in the next, thereby giving and seeking the afterlife rather than grieving over worldly loss.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r1.claim: This parable continues the warning against nullifying charity through reminders and harm; the garden owner has a small, weak family.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r2.claim: An i'sar is a violent whirlwind rising like a column; the burning whirlwind represents a hypocrite's or show-off's apparently good work being destroyed when most needed.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r3.claim: The elderly owner cannot restore the burned garden and his weak children cannot help him, leaving them helpless; likewise, the hypocrite's work is void when no aid, repentance, or reprieve remains.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r4.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p329/r4.claim: Ubayd ibn Umayr narrates that Umar asked the Companions who the garden parable concerned; Ibn Abbas said it represented a show-off, and Umar likened it to a wealthy worshipper whose sins destroy his deeds.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r1.claim: The opening hamza is interrogative for repudiation; the garden is said to consist of palms and vines for their excellence and abundance, with all fruits indicating the other kinds or benefits too.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r2.claim: The old age makes poverty and dependence more difficult, while weak offspring are too young to earn; the conjunction may be circumstantial or coordinated by sense.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r3.claim: An i'sar is a violent whirlwind rising from earth toward the sky like a column; the garden's fiery destruction pictures the anguish of finding good deeds nullified by ostentation or harm.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r4.claim: The parable also evokes someone who rises spiritually toward the divine realm, then turns back to worldly illusion and sees the effort scattered like dust.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:266/r5.claim: God explains the signs so people will think and draw a lesson from them.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r3.claim: The question expresses intense desire for an orchard, its inner space screened by trees; dates and grapes specify what the earlier garden parable left general.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r4.claim: The date palm is useful in its entirety, from its lasting leaves and nourishing fruit to its wood, resembling a believer whose whole person benefits others.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r5.claim: The grapevine branches upward, downward, and in every direction, resembling a pious believer honored through piety in every direction.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r6.claim: Running rivers indicate fertile, generous land; the author contrasts this irrigated garden with the earlier rain-fed ridge orchard, since irrigation failure costs more than rain-fed cultivation.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r7.claim: The garden's abundance includes every kind of fruit in addition to dates and grapes, making its destruction especially devastating.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p519/r8.claim: The owners children are young and weak, compounding his own weakness from old age and making the garden essential to his dependents.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r1.claim: Iʿṣār is an intensified form linked with squeezing out hidden contents; al-Ḥarālī describes a fierce wind within cloud, with a cold edge likened to one kind of fire.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r2.speaker: الأصفهاني
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r2.claim: Al-Aṣfahānī defines an iʿṣār as a wind that swirls across the ground and then rises toward the sky like a column.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r3.claim: The fiery whirlwind burns the garden and leaves its aged owner helpless, burdened with dependents and stripped of wealth; the analogy depicts ruin at the moment of greatest need.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r4.claim: The first garden image is ruined by an affliction from beneath, at the root; this one is struck from above, at the branches, marking two directions from which harm can come.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r5.claim: Someone who spoils charitable deeds through abuse faces a loss like the orchard owner and his family when their hopes are destroyed.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r6.speaker: عمر
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r6.claim: In a report recorded by al-Bukhārī in the tafsir, ʿUmar asks the Prophet's Companions what the garden verse means after they remain silent.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the garden as a person's deeds: a wealthy man obeys God, then Satan leads him into sins until they drown his deeds.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r8.claim: God clarifies all signs so people may reflect and benefit; the passage distinguishes those whose reflection multiplies their yield from those whose unconsidered actions let desire bring disaster.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r9.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r9.claim: Worship has no good without reflection; like a builder, a person must consider both the start and end of religious action, preparing its beginnings and later consequences.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r10.speaker: الحكيم
BIQAI-FULL:v1p520/r10.claim: A sage's maxim reverses the sequence of thought and action: the end of work is the beginning of thought, and the end of thought is the beginning of work.

DURR-FULL:v2p46/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p46/r12.claim: Asked by Umar about the garden parable, Ibn Abbas says it depicts a wealthy person who obeys God, then Satan draws him into sins that drown his deeds.

DURR-FULL:v2p47/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r1.speaker: عمر
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r1.claim: Umar invites Ibn Abbas to explain his whispered thought; Ibn Abbas says the parable concerns a deed, and Umar agrees it means a person's deeds needed most at old age and resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v2p47/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r2.claim: A person who spent youth doing good but becomes old with weak dependents, then loses his garden in a fiery storm, resembles a disbeliever left without good or help at resurrection.

DURR-FULL:v2p47/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r3.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r3.claim: The garden is a parable for ostentatious charity: at resurrection the donor needs his charity but finds showmanship has burned its reward.

DURR-FULL:v2p47/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r4.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r4.claim: It depicts someone who neglects obedience until death; old age and helpless children cannot help the ruined garden, just as all becomes regret after death.

DURR-FULL:v2p47/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r5.speaker: عمر
DURR-FULL:v2p47/r5.claim: Umar interprets the parable as a person doing good until late life, when he most needs his deeds, then committing evil.

DURR-FULL:v2p48/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r1.claim: The parable is a person who begins with good deeds but persists in sin late in life and dies in that state; the fiery whirlwind represents that final evil.

DURR-FULL:v2p48/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas tells Umar the garden means good work ruined by an evil final deed when a person most needs a good ending; Umar is struck by the interpretation.

DURR-FULL:v2p48/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r3.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r3.claim: The Prophet prayed that his broadest provision come in old age and near the end of his life.

DURR-FULL:v2p48/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r4.claim: An i'sar containing fire is a wind with intensely hot, scorching air.

DURR-FULL:v2p48/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r5.claim: In a lexical exchange with Ibn al-Azraq, he defines i'sar as a violent wind and cites Arabic poetry as evidence.

DURR-FULL:v2p48/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r6.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v2p48/r6.claim: God clarifies signs so people reflect; believers should understand the parables, as also stated at 29:43.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r1.speaker: الربيع
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r1.claim: Al-Rabi interprets the question as asking whether anyone would want to live in error and sin, die, and then find his deeds lost when he most needs them, as God asks what good he sent ahead.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r2.claim: Mujahid says the garden represents worldly life without obedience; after death, its owner is like an old man whose garden burns while his small children cannot help, just as the negligent person finds everything a regret.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the fruitful garden as what a person has fashioned or achieved in youth.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p522#2/r4.claim: In a discussion led by Umar, Ibn Abbas says the parable depicts a wealthy worshipper whose works are drowned after Satan leads him into sins; Umar accepts the interpretation as a parable for deeds.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r1.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r1.claim: Ikrima says the garden represents a person who worked in faith, good deeds, charity, and spending but committed shirk or a major sin at the end of life, voiding his deeds and dying an unbeliever.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r2.claim: Al-Suddi calls this another parable for ostentatious spending: the donor's money earns no reward and, when needed at the Resurrection, proves burned away like the garden.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r3.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r3.claim: Ikrima says every kind of tree in this world exists in Paradise, even colocynth.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the mention of weak offspring is part of the parable.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p523/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas expands the parable: a person's youthful work is lost in old age when a fiery whirlwind destroys his garden and weak children cannot help; likewise the unbeliever arrives before God with no good, while the believer's stored reward awaits him. He contrasts the believer's stored eternal honor with the wealthy unbeliever's lasting punishment for boasting and doubting the meeting with God.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the whirlwind as a wind; al-Suddi and al-Rabi are reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r2.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r2.claim: Al-Hasan gives a second gloss for the whirlwind: a cold blast or frost.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says the fire in the whirlwind is an intensely scorching wind; al-Suddi, Mujahid, and al-Rabi are reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r4.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r4.claim: Al-Hasan says the garden is lost precisely when its owner most needs it, illustrating deeds lost when they are most needed.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says the garden itself burned.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r6.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r6.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains “thus God makes the signs clear” as referring to what has just been mentioned.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r7.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r7.claim: Mujahid glosses “so that you may reflect” as “so that you may obey.”

IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r8.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p524/r8.claim: Qatada says this is a parable to be understood and pondered; only the learned grasp such parables, quoting 29:43.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r1.claim: The new parable answers the hearer's expectation after two favorable spending images, depicting the disgraceful opposite of sincere charity unaccompanied by reminders or harm.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r2.claim: Its likeness is failure and despair just as hope nears its harvest, contrasting the sincere spender and illustrating the ruin of showy or injurious giving.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r3.claim: The owner is old, unable to earn elsewhere, and has weak dependents; ضعيف means young or limited, and can also mean poor, as 2:282 and Abū Khālid al-ʿAttābī's verse show.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r4.claim: The poem of al-Aʿshā heightens the old man's dependence on his garden and anticipation of its yield, sharpening the audience's sense of impending loss.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p53#2/r5.claim: The destructive ʿiṣār is a violent hot wind, likened emphatically to fire or the simūm; it burns the garden's trees to dry wood and brings disaster at the moment of hope.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p54/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p54/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p54/r1.claim: أيود is a warning and repudiating question, like the question about eating a brother's flesh; the unstated analogue is someone whose charity is followed by reminders and harm.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p54/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p54/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p54/r2.claim: In the report of ʿUmar's question to the Companions, Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the garden as a wealthy person's good deeds, later consumed when Satan tempts him to sin near life's end; al-Bukhārī transmits the exchange.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p55/r1.claim: Likewise signals that God clarifies signs through this kind of explanation, bringing abstract truths near through tangible images so people reflect on consequences and avoid heedlessness.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r1.claim: من نخيل is a nominative adjective of garden; نخيل is either a collective noun or a plural of collective نخل.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r2.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r2.claim: Al-Rāghib derives نخيل from selected or sifted trees and calls it the noblest growth; he also notes its uses and human analogies.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r3.claim: أعناب is plural of عنبة; عنباء also occurs with a long final vowel and no declension.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r4.claim: The Qur’an names the palm tree but grape fruit: the whole palm is useful, while the vine’s chief benefit is its fruit.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266/r5.claim: تجري من تحتها may be a nominative adjective of garden, accusative circumstantial from its described noun, or a predicate of تكون according to Makkī.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r1.claim: In له فيها من كل الثمرات, له is predicate while من كل الثمرات appears to be the subject, requiring interpretation because a prepositional phrase is not literally a subject.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r2.claim: One solution supplies رزق or فاكهة, with the prepositional phrase standing as its adjective; al-Nābigha’s verse and 37:164 give parallels.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r3.speaker: الأخفش
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r3.claim: Another solution treats من as extra, yielding all fruits; since universal possession is impossible, كل means abundance rather than exhaustive totality. Al-Akhfash imposes no condition on extra من, unlike the Kūfan and Basran restrictions.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r4.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#2/r4.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ rejects extra من under both Sībawayh’s and al-Akhfash’s analysis because it would imply every fruit; he allows al-Akhfash’s analysis if abundance is meant.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r1.claim: وأصابه الكبر may be circumstantial with قد understood, attached to أحدكم and governed by يود; compare 2:28 and 3:168.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r2.speaker: الفراء
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r2.claim: The past may replace a present, ويصيبه, as in 11:98; al-Farrāʾ allows it after يود because that verb takes either أن or لو.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r3.claim: A third analysis coordinates by meaning: ‘would anyone wish that he had a garden and then old age struck him,’ converting present sense to past.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r4.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r4.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ considers the semantic coordination weak because it changes the wording despite an adequate sense.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r5.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r5.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī favors the semantic coordination as a question about having a garden and old age striking together.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r6.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r6.claim: Al-Shaykh objects that old age itself cannot be the object of someone’s wish, so it cannot coordinate with the wished-for garden.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#3/r7.claim: The objection is answered because the rhetorical question rejects the combined state of garden ownership and old age, not either element separately.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r1.claim: وله ذرية is circumstantial from the pronoun in وأصابه; ضعاف, ضعفاء, and ضِعاف are regular forms of ضعيف.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r2.claim: فأصابها إعصار coordinates with the earlier adjectival description of the garden, including من نخيل and what follows.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r3.claim: Repeated أصاب highlights impact on each target more strongly than simply saying rain, old age, or a whirlwind occurred.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r4.claim: إعصار is a strong rising wind, commonly called a whirlwind; al-Mahdawī reports ‘sirocco,’ explained by cloth-twisting or cloud-compressing.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r5.claim: Its plural is أعاصير, witnessed by the cited line; the wind-name is masculine, explaining فيه.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#4/r6.claim: In فيه نار, فيه may modify إعصار with نار as subject, or the clause may modify إعصار with نار as subject and فيه as predicate; the first is preferred because a simple adjective is nearer and preferable.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r1.claim: فاحترقت is the inchoative counterpart of causative أحرق: the garden was burned and then burned up.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r2.claim: حرق ناب الرجل means his anger intensified and can be transitive or intransitive; the cited line has نابه read nominative or accusative.

SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:266#5/r3.claim: The conclusion كذلك يبين الله لكم الآيات was discussed earlier.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r1.speaker: السدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r1.claim: Al-Suddī says this is another parable for ostentatious spending; al-Ṭabarī prefers that view.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd reads the verse as a parable continuing the command not to nullify charity through reproach and harm.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers Ibn Zayd’s contextual reading and rejects a second specific parable for ostentation; more broadly, the image fits any hypocrite or unbeliever who thinks he has done good but finds nothing at the moment of need.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r4.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r4.claim: When ʿUmar asked the Companions what the verse meant and they deferred to God and His Messenger, he angrily demanded that they say either that they knew or did not know.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās likens it to someone who does good throughout life but, near death, ends with the deeds of the damned; ʿUmar accepted this explanation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r6.speaker: ابن أبي مليكة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abī Mulayka reports that ʿUmar said the parable concerns one who does good until old age and then does evil when most in need of the good deeds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r7.claim: The broad reading includes whatever the wording can cover; Mujāhid, Qatāda, and al-Rabīʿ share this general interpretation.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r8.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والربيع وغيرهم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r8.claim: They give an interpretation along these lines of a person’s good works being undone at the end.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r9.claim: Palms and grapevines are named for their superior standing among trees.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r10.speaker: الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r10.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads the word for garden in the plural.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r11.claim: “From beneath them” means below the trees; the wāw in “and old age came upon him” and “he has weak offspring” introduces circumstantial clauses.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r12.claim: The wāw introduces a circumstantial clause, and ḍuʿafāʾ and ḍiʿāf are plural forms of ḍaʿīf.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r13.claim: A Prophetic report says that intense heat is from Hell’s breath and that the Fire complained to its Lord.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p360#2/r14.claim: The iʿṣār is a violent, scorching wind that burns what it passes over.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r1.claim: The whirlwind’s fire may be literal, or it may be Hell’s breath producing a similar effect.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r2.speaker: السدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r2.claim: Al-Suddī says the whirlwind is wind and its fire is the scorching samūm wind.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās describes it as a wind containing severe samūm.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r4.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says the samūm from which jinn were created is one part in seventy of the Fire.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r5.claim: He clarifies that Ibn Masʿūd means the fire of the afterlife.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r6.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r6.claim: Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan defines it as a whirlwind carrying cold, biting wind; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the same.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r7.speaker: الضحاك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r7.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk shares the interpretation of the whirlwind as carrying cold, biting wind.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r8.claim: A proverb says that if one is a wind, one has met a whirlwind; the name may relate to the wind squeezing or twisting clouds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r9.claim: Muʿṣirāt may mean clouds carrying rain like women ready for childbirth, or clouds compressed by winds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r10.speaker: عبيد الله بن الحسن العنبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r10.claim: The judge ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan al-ʿAnbarī interprets the clouds as being compressed by the winds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r11.speaker: ابن سيده
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r11.claim: Ibn Sīda reports that some exegetes explain muʿṣirāt as winds rather than clouds.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r12.speaker: الزجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r12.claim: Al-Zajjāj defines an iʿṣār as a violent wind rising from earth to sky, called a zawbaʿa.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r13.speaker: المهدوي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r13.claim: Al-Mahdawī says the wind is called an iʿṣār because it twists like cloth being wrung; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this explanation weak.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r14.claim: He regards the derivation from cloth being wrung as weak.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r15.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r15.claim: “Thus” points to the parables just described; “perhaps” expresses hope from a human perspective, since reflection may make a person fit to think.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r16.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p361/r16.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says people are to reflect on the world’s passing away and the afterlife’s arrival and permanence.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r1.claim: This parable continues the warning not to nullify charity in 2:264; awadda means “would love.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r2.claim: Dates and grapes represent the most precious orchard produce; old age is singled out because the person may have lost the ability to earn as in youth.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r3.claim: A person's weak offspring make that parent especially tender and protective toward them.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r4.claim: An ʿiṣār is a fierce whirlwind that carries dust upward like a column.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r5.claim: An unnamed poet says that whoever is a wind has met a tornado, meaning someone still stronger.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r6.speaker: الفراء وثعلب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r6.claim: The past-tense wording for the garden and storm is permissible with wadd, since Arabs alternate between an and law after “I wished.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r7.claim: The parable depicts the anguish of losing a blessing at the moment of greatest need.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r8.claim: One interpretation makes the garden owner a person whose life ends in corruption.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r9.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r9.claim: Another interpretation is a person who neglects obedience to God until death.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r10.speaker: السدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p320#2/r10.claim: The garden represents ostentatious charity whose benefit disappears when the giver most needs it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r1.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r1.claim: Umar asks the Companions whom the garden parable concerns, then presses them to say whether they know.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the garden as a wealthy person’s good deeds later drowned by sins after Satan turns him toward disobedience.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r3.claim: The parable warns of someone who began well, then replaced good deeds with sins and found no earlier good when most in need.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r4.claim: An ʿiṣār is a fierce wind; its fire burns the garden’s fruit and destroys its trees, leaving the elderly owner helpless.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r5.claim: An alternate Ibn Abbas report depicts a man wasting his garden in youth, then losing it in old age when weak children cannot restore or support him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r6.claim: The ruined garden parallels the disbeliever at resurrection: he has no good to seek renewed standing and loses reward when most desperate for it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p695#3/r7.claim: Ibn Kathir notes that this interpretation is reported by al-Bukhari alone.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p696/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p696/r1.speaker: رسول الله
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p696/r1.claim: Al-Hakim reports the Prophet praying that his broadest provision come in old age and near the end of life.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p696/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p696/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p696/r2.claim: The signs teach readers to consider and understand parables, then apply them to their intended meanings.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r1.claim: The interrogative hamza expresses disapproval; readings also have ‘gardens’ and ‘weak offspring.’

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r2.claim: An iʿṣār is a rotating wind that rises from the ground like a column into the sky.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r3.claim: The image concerns good deeds done without seeking God: on Judgment Day they are found void, producing the devastation of an elderly person whose dependent children lose their livelihood.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r4.claim: Asked by Umar, Ibn Abbas interprets the image as a wealthy person whose good deeds are later drowned by sins after Satan leads him astray.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r5.speaker: الحسن
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341/r5.claim: Al-Hasan says the old person with many children is most in need of his garden, just as a believer is most in need of his deeds when worldly life ends.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r1.claim: Palms and vines are singled out as the noblest and most useful trees, though the garden contains others; all fruits are then added.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r2.claim: Fruits may mean all the benefits of the garden, as in the story of the two gardens in al-Kahf.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p341#2/r3.claim: The conjunction before ‘old age struck him’ can be circumstantial; alternatively, the wording follows the meaning of ‘would one wish if he had a garden and had grown old?’

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r1.claim: Janna means orchard; palms and grapes are among its finest contents, and its best feature is flowing water.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r2.claim: Old age can make a person forget the effort of youth, leaving him with weaker hopes and greater regret.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r3.claim: An elderly person is more tender and solicitous toward weak children.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r4.speaker: السدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r4.claim: Al-Suddi says an i'sar is the lethal hot wind called samum; another account describes a whirlwind rising like a column from earth to sky, commonly called zawbaa.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r5.claim: The whirlwind is called i'sar because it spirals like cloth being wrung; a cited poem uses the term.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r6.claim: God's explaining the signs can mean clarifying proofs or giving parables; reflection means taking a lesson or finding guidance.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r7.speaker: السدي
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r7.claim: Al-Suddi says the burning garden pictures a show-off whose spending benefit disappears when he needs it most.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r8.speaker: مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r8.claim: Mujahid interprets the image as one who neglects obedience for worldly pleasures and faces immense regret in the afterlife.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p340#2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas says the image is of someone who ends his work with corruption.

MUQATIL:2:266/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:266/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:266/r1.claim: The garden is a parable for a disbeliever's deeds: an old man with helpless young children loses their livelihood to a fiery hot wind and cannot restore it.

MUQATIL:2:266/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:266/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:266/r2.claim: The disbeliever has stored no good for the afterlife when most in need of it, just as the old man loses his garden when he and his children most need it.

MUQATIL:2:266/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:266/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:266/r3.claim: The disbeliever cannot return to worldly life to make amends, just as the old man cannot become young again and replant the garden; the parable invites reflection.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r1.claim: The interrogative hamza expresses denial of the prospect of such a loss.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r2.claim: The garden is described with dates and grapes because they are the noblest, most beneficial trees; all fruits are then added by generalization.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r3.claim: The conjunction before old age is circumstantial, as is the clause about weak offspring; the garden is the aged owner's livelihood and theirs.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r4.claim: An iʿṣār is a whirlwind that rotates over the ground and rises skyward like a column; fire is raised by the ظرف because the ظرف functions as an adjective of the whirlwind.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r5.claim: The garden's destruction depicts ostentatious good deeds found null at resurrection, causing the anguish of an elderly person whose weak children depend on the ruined garden.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p130#2/r6.claim: As with the preceding explanation of monotheism and religion, the signs are clarified to prompt reflection and awaken people.

ZAJJAJ:v1p347#2/r8.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p347#2/r8.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p347#2/r8.claim: The ruined orchard is a parable for the afterlife: losing the deeds that would lead to Paradise leaves an elderly person with vulnerable dependents in the same desperate position as losing his garden.

ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r1.claim: An ʿiṣār is a fierce whirlwind rising like a column from earth toward the sky, called zawbaʿa; an unnamed poetic line illustrates it.

ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r2.speaker: الشاعر
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r2.claim: An unnamed poet uses iʿṣār for a whirlwind met by the wind.

ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p349/r3.claim: God’s clarification encompasses the earlier charity, struggle, Abraham, and ruined-town examples, which mark the evidence needed concerning oneness, messengership, reward, and punishment.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r1.speaker: السدي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r1.claim: Al-Suddi, preferred by al-Tabari, takes the garden as a second parable for ostentatious spending; Ibn Abbas also reports a likeness to deeds of show-offs that are void when most needed.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd connects the garden directly to the prohibition against nullifying charity with reminders and harm in 2:264.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r3.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the connection to the preceding context is clearer than treating this as a separate parable for ostentatious spending; more broadly it covers any hypocrite or disbeliever whose apparent good deed vanishes when needed.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r4.claim: In the established Bukhari report, Ibn Abbas says the garden represents a wealthy person who obeys God, then follows Satan into sins until his life's work is burned away; Umar approves the explanation.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r5.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r5.claim: Umar asks the Companions what the garden verse means, urges them to answer rather than defer, and accepts Ibn Abbas's interpretation; another report says a person may end a righteous life with evil deeds when he most needs his work.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r6.speaker: ابن أبي مليكة
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r6.claim: Ibn Abi Mulayka reports Umar explaining that someone may do good until old age but commit evil at the end of life, when he most needs his good deeds.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r7.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r7.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, al-Rabi, and others support a broad reading that applies to every case covered by the wording.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r8.claim: Palms and grapes are singled out because they are superior and especially prized among trees; 'all fruits' means every kind grows there.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266/r9.claim: The past-tense 'old age struck him' is coordinated with the future 'that he should have'; alternative analyses link it to 'would wish,' treat it as circumstantial, or understand an implicit 'if he had a garden.'

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r1.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r1.claim: Al-Hasan says an iʿṣār with fire is a wind containing intense cold.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines iʿṣār as a powerful whirlwind rising from the ground like a column, called a zawbaʿa.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r3.speaker: الجوهري
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r3.claim: Al-Jawhari says a whirlwind is also called zawbaʿa or umm zawbaʿa; the term also names a chief of the jinn.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r4.speaker: المهدوي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r4.claim: Al-Mahdawi says the wind is called iʿṣār because it twists like cloth when wrung; Ibn Atiyya calls this weak, but the author endorses it as the observable coiling column.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r5.claim: The author regards the twisting-column explanation as sound because it matches what can be seen.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r6.claim: Other derivations say the wind squeezes clouds, or that muʿṣirāt are pregnant clouds or clouds compressed by winds; Ibn Sidah says some took muʿṣirāt to mean winds.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r7.claim: Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi describe the iʿṣār as a violent, scorching wind; Ibn Abbas calls it a wind with intense samūm heat.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r8.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r8.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the whirlwind's intense heat or cold is a breath of Hell, citing Prophetic reports about delaying prayer in severe heat and the Fire's complaint.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas and others explain the parable as a disbeliever's or hypocrite's livelihood orchard burning when its elderly owner and weak children can neither replace nor sustain it; the afterlife offers no second chance to restore deeds.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas also says the closing appeal is to reflect on the world's passing and the afterlife's arrival and permanence.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:266#2/r11.claim: The appeal to reflect also means returning to God's majesty and lordship rather than taking protectors besides Him.

RAZI-FULL:v7p51#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p51#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p51#2/r1.claim: The garden parable depicts a person who is old, unable to earn, and responsible for helpless dependents; losing the garden to a fiery whirlwind leaves desperate need and regret, like a deed nullified by reproach at Judgment.

RAZI-FULL:v7p51#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p51#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p51#2/r2.claim: Wudd means complete love; the interrogative is repudiative, and the verse uses it because the desire to avoid such calamity would be maximally intense.

RAZI-FULL:v7p52/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p52/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p52/r1.claim: The garden's palms and grapes are singled out as noble, attractive fruits; rivers and every kind of produce complete a garden of unsurpassable beauty and usefulness.

RAZI-FULL:v7p52/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p52/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p52/r2.claim: Old age increases needs while reducing earning capacity, and young children add dependency; the waw before أصابه is circumstantial per al-Kashshāf or semantically conditional per al-Farrāʾ.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r1.claim: An iʿṣār is a very strong whirlwind rising and rotating skyward like a column, called a whirlwind locally; an unnamed poet's line confirms the image.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r2.claim: The burned garden represents ostensibly good acts done without God's pleasure or with corrupting additions; at Judgment their needy owner discovers the acts cannot help, as in al-Zumar 39:47 and al-Furqān 25:23.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r3.claim: Just as God explains these signs with encouragement and warning, He explains signs across religion so people may reflect.

RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p53/r4.claim: Al-Rāzī notes that لعل is a particle of hope inappropriate to God and reports the Muʿtazilite argument that the verse implies God intended all people to believe.

STUDYQURAN:2:266/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r1.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r1.claim: R reads the garden as charity’s fruit and the fiery whirlwind as later boasting and insults that destroy it, leaving the giver with nothing for the Hereafter or weak descendants to support him.

STUDYQURAN:2:266/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r2.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the verse as people doing good works and later evil works that wipe out the earlier deeds’ value.

STUDYQURAN:2:266/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r3.claim: Every kind of fruit may mean many kinds of fruit.

STUDYQURAN:2:266/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:266/r4.claim: Rivers running below is a common image for Paradise.

TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r1.claim: The parable depicts a hypocrite's showy charity: it wins worldly praise, protection, and other benefits, like a fruitful garden.

TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r2.claim: The garden's destruction in old age, when the owner has weak children and needs its fruit most, represents ostentation extinguishing his reward when he most needs it, with no repentance then.

TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r3.claim: This parable is the counterpart of the stone covered with soil that rain leaves bare in the preceding verse.

TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p679#2/r4.claim: Although exegetes vary in wording, al-Suddī gives the clearest and closest-to-correct explanation.

TAB-FULL:v4p682/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p682/r1.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p682/r1.claim: Al-Suddī calls this another parable for ostentatious charity: its apparent merit is burned away when the giver needs it at Judgment.

TAB-FULL:v4p682/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p682/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p682/r2.claim: Mujāhid compares neglecting obedience until death to a garden destroyed after its owner grows old; after death everything becomes regret.

TAB-FULL:v4p682/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p682/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p682/r3.claim: In answer to ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās says a person may do good until old age and then end with an act of the wretched, ruining all his work when most needed.

TAB-FULL:v4p684/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r1.speaker: عمر
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r1.claim: ʿUmar reads the parable as someone doing good until late in life, then committing evil at the point he most needs his good works.

TAB-FULL:v4p684/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the garden as a person's good works: later sins can burn them away, leaving no recourse after death.

TAB-FULL:v4p684/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r3.speaker: عطاء ومجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r3.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and Mujāhid say the garden is a parable for deeds.

TAB-FULL:v4p684/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r4.claim: Mujāhid says the parable concerns the person who neglects obedience until death.

TAB-FULL:v4p684/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p684/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the destroyed garden is the person's livelihood and his children's; like it, he cannot rebuild or repent once work ends at death.

TAB-FULL:v4p687/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r1.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r1.claim: Mujāhid again interprets the scene as worldly life without obedience and the regret of the negligent after death.

TAB-FULL:v4p687/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r2.claim: Qatāda urges people to understand God's parables and asks whether anyone would want his deeds lost on Judgment Day when most needed; he cites 29:43.

TAB-FULL:v4p687/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r3.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the garden vanished at the greatest need, just as a person's deeds may disappear when most needed.

TAB-FULL:v4p687/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p687/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās contrasts the believer's stored afterlife honor with the disbeliever's temporary wealth and lasting punishment, incurred through pride and lack of certainty in meeting God.

TAB-FULL:v4p688/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r1.speaker: الربيع
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r1.claim: Al-Rabīʿ says the parable warns against living in error and sin until death, when one's work is most needed but has vanished.

TAB-FULL:v4p688/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd connects the garden parable to the preceding warning against invalidating alms with reminders and harm.

TAB-FULL:v4p688/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r3.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r3.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk calls the garden a parable for the disbeliever, who arrives needing good but finds none and cannot avert punishment.

TAB-FULL:v4p688/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r4.claim: The context makes this a parable for those who remind or hurt charity recipients, like the immediately preceding hypocrite example, rather than an unrelated subject.

TAB-FULL:v4p688/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p688/r5.claim: The past-tense أصابه follows أيود because أن and an implied لو both convey a future condition, allowing a past verb under the لو construction.

TAB-FULL:v4p690/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r1.claim: فعيل can pluralize as فعلاء or فعال, explaining ضعفاء here and the form ضعافا in 4:9.

TAB-FULL:v4p690/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r2.claim: An إعصار is a violent wind rising from earth toward the sky like a column; its plural is أعاصير.

TAB-FULL:v4p690/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r3.claim: Yazīd ibn Mufarrigh al-Ḥimyarī's verse uses أعاصير as evidence for the word's meaning.

TAB-FULL:v4p690/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the fire in the whirlwind as intensely hot samūm wind.

TAB-FULL:v4p690/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p690/r5.claim: A further report from Ibn ʿAbbās says the samūm from which jinn were created is one seventieth of fire.

TAB-FULL:v4p693/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the fiery whirlwind as intensely scorching samūm.

TAB-FULL:v4p693/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r2.claim: Qatāda says the whirlwind is a wind carrying intense samūm.

TAB-FULL:v4p693/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r3.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r3.claim: Al-Suddī distinguishes the whirlwind as wind and its fire as samūm.

TAB-FULL:v4p693/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r4.speaker: الحسن
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan offers a competing explanation: the whirlwind contains severe cold and hail.

TAB-FULL:v4p693/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r5.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p693/r5.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise interprets the whirlwind as a wind containing cold.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.claim: The connected themes suggest this passage was revealed as one unit: spending grows seven hundredfold or more, sincere giving bears fruit, ostentation and reminders or harm ruin reward, good wealth should be given, the poor detained in God's path are recipients, and the reward is great.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.claim: The passage orders its teaching around purpose (giving for God, not people), manner (without reproach or injury), quality (good rather than bad wealth), recipient (the needy constrained in God's path), and reward.

TABATABAI:2:265-266/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r5.claim: Wudd is love with an element of wishing; janna is dense tree growth that covers and shades the earth, so rivers flow beneath the garden rather than beneath the land itself.

TABATABAI:2:265-266/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:265-266/r6.claim: This reading of garden accords with 23:50, which describes a settled elevation with flowing water, and with the repeated image of gardens whose water flows below them.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r1.claim: Min in 'of palms and grapes' explains the garden's predominant crop rather than excluding other plants; that is why the verse adds that it contains every kind of fruit.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r2.claim: Old age together with weak children makes the garden an indispensable source of livelihood: a young owner, a childless elder, or an elder with strong children could each fall back on another means.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r3.claim: When an elderly owner with frail children loses the garden to fire, neither he nor they can restore their strength, former resources, or the lost orchard, leaving them without a means or hope.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r4.claim: An iʿṣār is a column of dust twisting between sky and earth, like cloth twisted during wringing.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r5.claim: The ruined-garden parable depicts charity nullified by reminders and harm: a spoiled deed cannot be restored to soundness.

TABATABAI:2:266-267/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:266-267/r6.claim: Such corruption comes from inner loves of wealth and status, pride, conceit, and miserliness that block reflection and discernment; contemplation would expose the harm.

TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r6.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
TABATABAI:2:261-274#7/r6.claim: Al-Qummī glosses ṣafwān as a large rock, wābil as rain, tall as nighttime dew on plants, and iʿṣār as winds.

TABRISI:2:266/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266/r1.claim: جنة is a densely planted garden; نخيل is sometimes explained from sifting and selecting, and نخلة names a date tree; the word may be masculine or feminine.

TABRISI:2:266/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266/r2.claim: An orchard has fruit trees and running waterways; كبير means age or magnitude, while كثير specifically implies number; إعصار is a twisting column of dust or wind.

TABRISI:2:266/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266/r3.claim: الأنهار names broad channels of flowing water; التحوت refers to people low under others' feet and unnoticed.

TABRISI:2:266/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266/r4.speaker: author
