TABRISI:2:266/r4.claim: The poem compares a powerful whirlwind with another whirlwind, illustrating إعصار.

TABRISI:2:266/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266/r5.claim: The expression كبير differs from كثير: كبير describes size even for one house, whereas كثير necessarily implies number.

TABRISI:2:266#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266#2/r1.claim: مِن in من نخيل explains the garden's type; the clause about running rivers can modify either the garden or the date palms, depending on the pronoun's antecedent.

TABRISI:2:266#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266#2/r2.claim: The parable imagines an orchard of date palms and grapes, with water and every fruit, possessed by an aging person with weak, young children.

TABRISI:2:266#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266#2/r3.claim: إعصار is a powerful, upward-spinning wind column, commonly called a whirlwind; fire in it burns the garden.

TABRISI:2:266#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266#2/r4.speaker: السدي
TABRISI:2:266#2/r4.claim: Al-Suddi sees the ruined garden as the show-off in spending: he enjoys its benefit now but loses it when he most needs the reward in the hereafter.

TABRISI:2:266#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266#2/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:2:266#2/r5.claim: Mujahid reads the garden as the person who neglects obedience for worldly pleasures and thus faces especially bitter regret when he needs righteous deeds in the hereafter.

TABRISI:2:266#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:2:266#2/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets it as someone whose work ends in corruption; the author says all three interpretations fit the verse.

TABRISI:2:266#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:266#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:266#2/r7.claim: The explanation points back to charity, Abraham's story, the passerby at the ruined village, and all prior disclosures; God sets out religious proofs so people will reflect and understand.

THALABI:v2p264/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p264/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p264/r10.claim: The garden parable in 2:266 connects back to the prohibition on nullifying charity with reproach and harm.

THALABI:v2p264/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p264/r11.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p264/r11.claim: The past verb aṣābahu follows a future construction because Arabic permits widad with either past-like law or future-like an; they can be interchanged in this sense.

THALABI:v2p265/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p265/r1.claim: Because law and an may substitute for each other after wishing, aṣābahā is understood as a future event, even though it is expressed in the past; a line of poetry illustrates the construction.

THALABI:v2p265/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p265/r2.claim: The parable's owner is old and has weak, helpless young children; an iʿṣār is a rising whirlwind like a column, and its plural is aʿāṣīr.

THALABI:v2p265/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r3.speaker: الكميت
THALABI:v2p265/r3.claim: Al-Kumayt's lines use iʿṣār for a forceful, dust-bearing whirlwind, as a lexical witness.

THALABI:v2p265/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r4.speaker: يزيد بن المقرع الحميري
THALABI:v2p265/r4.claim: Yazīd ibn al-Muqriʿ al-Ḥimyarī uses the plural aʿāṣīr in a poem as further evidence for the word.

THALABI:v2p265/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p265/r5.claim: The parable depicts a hypocritical show-off who expects benefit from his work, but loses it in old age when he and his helpless children cannot restore the burned garden; so the work is voided when repentance is no longer possible.

THALABI:v2p265/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p265/r6.speaker: عبيد بن عمير
THALABI:v2p265/r6.claim: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr instead applies the parable to someone who begins with righteous work, later persists in evil, and dies in that state; the fire-filled whirlwind represents the final evil.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r1.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r1.claim: They connect this parable to 2:264: it pictures ostentatious spending that is nullified by reproach and harm.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r2.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r2.claim: He sees a person neglecting obedience to God and occupied with worldly pleasures, only to face immense regret in the afterlife.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r3.claim: He sees someone who ends a good life with corruption: Satan leads him into sin late in life until he dies in it, like the fiery whirlwind destroying the orchard.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r4.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r4.claim: He explains past وأصابه الكبر after future أيود through the near-equivalent conditional particles أن and لو; examples occur in 2:221, 30:51, and 68:9.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r5.claim: An إعصار is a strong rotating wind rising like a column, also called a whirlwind; Ibn al-Aʿrabi records عصار and its use for a dust-raising wind.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r6.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p420/r6.claim: The man is old and unable to work, with dependent young children; fire destroys his orchard when he needs it most, leaving the family helpless, just as hypocrites' deeds are nullified when repentance is no longer possible.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p421/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p421/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p421/r1.claim: God explains signs through accounts such as the passerby at the ruined town and Abraham, clarifying the proofs people need concerning divine oneness.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r1.claim: The orchard owner is old and unable to earn, has dependent young children, and loses his fruit garden to a fiery whirlwind when he needs it most.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r2.claim: The owner and children are helpless and bewildered; similarly, God nullifies hypocrites' and show-offs' deeds, leaving them no repentance or reprieve from their sins.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:266-267/r3.claim: The verse's explanatory stories clarify God's signs concerning his oneness.

ELMALILI:2:266/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:266/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:266/r1.claim: The image asks whether anyone would want a rich orchard to burn just when old age and helpless young dependents make its loss devastating.

ELMALILI:2:266/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:266/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:266/r2.claim: Faith and good deeds are like gardens whose reward is destroyed at Judgment by disbelief, ostentation, reminders, hurt, and other corrupt motives.

ELMALILI:2:266/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:266/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:266/r3.claim: The Islamic polity is also a garden that prepares the way to eternal blessing; coercive, unbelieving injustice, immorality, and loss of resolve can devastate both worldly life and the afterlife.

ELMALILI:2:266/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:266/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:266/r4.claim: God explains signs so people reflect, draw sound analogies from them, apply principles to their circumstances, reach conclusions, and act toward their aims.

ELMALILI:2:266/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:266/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:266/r5.claim: Thought is the process of arranging known matters to discover what is unknown.

ELMALILI:2:266/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:266/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:266/r6.claim: The discussion turns toward where, how, and to whom obligatory and voluntary spending should be given.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:265/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:265/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:265/r2.claim: Charity given for other purposes reduces wealth but earns no reward; at the afterlife, the donor is left empty-handed like an old man whose orchard burns just when he needs it.
